intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35), also known as tyrosine kinase-2 (TYK2) deficiency, is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TYK2 gene.

paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency. Its core feature is susceptibility to intracellular bacteria, such as BCG and other mycobacteria, Salmonella, and Brucella, and/or to viruses, particularly herpesviruses. The first reported patient was diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) because he had atopic dermatitis, high serum IgE, and staphylococcal infections (Minegishi et al., 2006). Most later patients have had no features of HIES (Kreins et al., 2015). Patient cells show impaired but not abolished responses to IL-12, IL-23, IFN-alpha/beta, and IL-10 (Kreins et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Minegishi et al. (2006) reported a patient who had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome. He had unusual susceptibility to viruses, fungi, and mycobacteria, and atopic dermatitis with elevated serum IgE. Kreins et al. (2015) gave further details of this patient (P1), a Japanese man born to consanguineous parents. He had atopic dermatitis from age 1 month and recurrent bacterial and viral infections from age 1 year. At 22 months, 6 months after vaccination, he developed BCGitis. He had repeated skin abscesses caused by S. aureus, pneumonia without pneumatocele formation, otitis, and sinusitis. At 15 years he developed sepsis after severe nontyphi Salmonella enterocolitis. Viral infections included parainfluenza virus-3 pneumonia, recurrent oral HSV infections with tonsillitis, and molluscum contagiosum. He also had mild oral candidiasis. Investigations repeatedly showed hypereosinophilia (701-800/microliter) and high serum IgE (1,430-2,100 IU/ml), and he had an NIH HIES score of 48. Kilic et al. (2012) noted that he had no bone fractures and that his dentition and facial appearance were normal.

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy with IMD35 born to first-cousin parents. He received BCG vaccine at 2 months. Left axillary lymphadenopathy appeared at 8 months, and by 21 months he had generalized lymphadenopathy and fatigue. At 2 years he had fever and fistulous bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy, and M. bovis BCG was isolated from the draining cervical sinuses. At 8 years he developed Brucella meningitis (neurobrucellosis) with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. This was followed by severe hearing loss, severe cognitive impairment, and lacunar infarcts on MRI. At 11 years he had herpes zoster of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve. He had no atopy, staphylococcal infection, candidiasis, or skeletal or dental features of HIES. Serum IgE was 80, 115, 218, and 155 IU/ml at ages 2, 11, 16, and 18 years, respectively.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) reported 7 further TYK2-deficient patients (P2-P8) from 5 families. P2 was the Turkish patient reported by Kilic et al. (2012). P3, a Moroccan girl born to first-cousin parents, was hospitalized at 13 years with suspected abdominal tuberculosis and later had disseminated extrapulmonary tuberculosis with ascites and a psoas abscess. She died of bacterial meningitis 15 months after symptom onset. Her brother (P4) had meningitis of unknown etiology at 8 months, recurrent otitis and urinary tract infections, asthma, eczema of the ear canal, and high eosinophil levels. P5, a boy born to consanguineous Iranian parents, had BCG lymphadenitis at 2 and 4 months. At 4.5 years he developed paravertebral and psoas abscesses with pulmonary involvement. His younger sister (P6) had BCG lymphadenopathy and, at 1 year, an unidentified viral skin infection. P7, a 9-year-old Iranian girl born to consanguineous parents, had miliary tuberculosis. P8, an 11-year-old boy from Argentina, had recurrent herpes gingivostomatitis, aseptic herpes meningitis, and disseminated cutaneous herpetic lesions. He also had mild mental disability that may have been congenital or postmeningitic. None of P2-P8 had documented staphylococcal or fungal infections, and serum IgE was never high.

paragraphs.text: Wu et al. (2020) reported a Chinese boy with IMD35 born to nonconsanguineous parents. After BCG vaccination on day 3 of life, he had repeated abscess and ulceration at the injection site, which healed by 10 months. At 14 months he developed BCG lymph node tuberculosis in the left axilla. From age 6 months he had recurrent respiratory tract infections and diarrhea. Pathogens found during his admissions included Salmonella, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and M. bovis BCG, and IgM antibodies to influenza A and B viruses were positive. He had no high serum IgE, atopy, or staphylococcal disease. He spoke his first simple words at 3 years 4 months, and his head circumference was small. Natural killer cells were reduced (3.6%) and CD19+ B cells were increased (26.6%).

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2022) identified 3 unrelated Turkish children with COVID-19 pneumonia in an international cohort of 112 children hospitalized for the disease. They were a 2-year-old girl and boys aged 4 and 9 years, each born to consanguineous parents. The girl had moderate pneumonia, and the 2 boys had critical pneumonia requiring ICU admission. Earlier, the girl had been hospitalized for infection from a live viral vaccine, the 4-year-old boy had been admitted to the ICU for influenza pneumonia at 3 years, and the 9-year-old boy had recurrent bronchitis. The 3-year-old sister of the 4-year-old boy carried the same genotype.
